The code confirms the executor lifecycle. It strongly suggests a cause for the observed throughput and CPU gap, but a CPU profile is still needed to attribute the exact cost. The benchmark uses sleeping tasks as a proxy for waiting on I/O. Review sources: the supplied k6 screenshot and ConcurrentTaskService.java in each of java17, java21, and java25.

Sources: BenchmarkController.java and ConcurrentTaskService.java in all three modules, plus k6/ramp-up.js. The tasks execute concurrently, so the intended wait is about 100 ms per request rather than 50 times 100 ms. Additional execution, scheduling, HTTP, and completion overhead remains.

Source: java17/src/main/java/com/meutudo/benchmarkjava17/ConcurrentTaskService.java lines 17–31. The snippet omits submission details for readability. A fresh fixed pool starts workers as tasks are submitted. Here 50 submissions to a fresh pool with 50 core workers result in 50 workers during a successful call. There is no single global 50-worker task queue. API reference: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/Executors.html#newFixedThreadPool(int)

Sources: Java 17 screenshot throughput and the confirmed per-request pool implementation. The approximate creation rate assumes successful calls submit the configured 50 tasks. 102.235122 times 50 is about 5,112 threads/second over the aggregate run. The 10,000 figure is potential concurrent task-thread demand if 200 HTTP requests are simultaneously executing this service. It is not 10,000 tasks per second and is not a measured live thread count.

Observed evidence: user CPU annotations in the screenshot, not k6 measurements. Code evidence: fresh native worker pools per request. Attribution to creation, scheduling, allocation, or cleanup remains a hypothesis until measured. A sleeping OS thread is not continuously runnable, so a large live thread count alone does not prove constant scheduler thrashing. Do not attribute all CPU usage to context switching. CPU scales vary across operating-system monitors, Docker, and normalized JVM metrics. API reference: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Thread.html#sleep(long)

Sources: java21 and java25 ConcurrentTaskService.java, executor creation at line 17. Each executor starts one virtual thread per task and does not create a new private OS carrier pool for every request. Oracle's virtual-thread guide explains suspension and carrier reuse, and states that virtual threads improve throughput and scale rather than individual CPU execution speed. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/core/virtual-threads.html Implementation reference for sleep and scheduling: https://openjdk.org/jeps/444

Sources: screenshot scenario text and k6/ramp-up.js. Each enabled iteration issues one synchronous HTTP request and has no explicit sleep. The screenshot shows one stage lasting one minute. At slide creation, the locally modified script shows a two-minute ramp, so it is not an exact reproduction of the screenshot configuration. VU counts and average response times vary throughout the run. Avoid substituting the maximum 200 users into this formula to predict aggregate throughput.

Sources: service implementations and application.properties. Java 21 and 25 set spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true, Java 17 has no such setting. The current build.gradle files all use Spring Boot 3.5.16, contrary to older README descriptions, so this deck does not attribute the gap to different Spring Boot versions. Changing Spring's virtual-thread setting can also change request handling, beyond the explicit executor inside the service. Spring reference: https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/3.5/reference/features/task-execution-and-scheduling.html

Proposed validation, not completed testing. Keep workload parameters, Spring Boot, HTTP threading configuration where applicable, CPU/memory limits, JVM flags, and monitoring scales consistent. Shared-pool capacity must be declared because reducing native thread creation also introduces a concurrency limit and queueing. Verify actual java -version in each running process/container. Repeated separate runs reduce interference and establish variability.

Evidence summary: source inspection confirms the per-request pool and virtual-thread alternative. Screenshot measurements confirm the throughput and latency gap in this run. The CPU breakdown remains unmeasured. No application changes or new benchmark runs form part of this presentation. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/core/virtual-threads.html
